answer.rationale: The 18% spend cut and the incumbent's refusal to reopen price eliminate negotiate_terms and renew_incumbent as viable paths; memory_c4's margin recovery via benchmarking cannot apply when the incumbent has explicitly closed price discussion this cycle. Deferring (memory_c5 pattern) is ruled out because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew and the assembly line is already at 94% with no buffer—any gap in supply escalates immediately to a delivery failure. Adding a second source (memory_c3) addresses resilience but does not meet the cost mandate and consumes the single decision slot without touching unit price. Switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor is the only candidate that attacks the 18% cut target directly. Memory_c2 records that the prior switch cut unit cost sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate—meaning the transition risk was contained. I am pulling memory_c2 to confirm those onboarding and accuracy details still hold, and memory_c4 to verify whether any benchmarking data compiled during that renegotiation gives me current market-rate leverage with the incoming vendor. Memory_c1 (incumbent stability) and memory_c6 (multi-year volume pricing) are noted as evidence of what we are forgoing, but both depend on the incumbent being willing to engage on terms, which they have refused. Delivery risk is mitigated by the 14-day window matching the quick-onboarding pattern in memory_c2 and by the fact that no contract change happens mid-stream. No other decision this cycle can satisfy both the cost mandate and the delivery constraint simultaneously.
